references.title: TEDx Speaker Guide
references.note: Organiser's guide for TEDx speakers: under 18 minutes, one idea, an invisible structure, no pitch at the close, rehearse as one-to-one talk. Rules from the programme's experience, with no data.

references.title: How to Give a Toast
references.note: Short tip page, no evidence: two to three minutes, one main idea, a brief story or quality, a clear invitation to drink, notecards and rehearsal. Its sample toasts are generic templates.

references.title: Delivering Eulogies
references.note: Five tip bullets, no evidence and no length: write it out and practise, two or three main points, a tribute and not a chronology, restrained gestures.

references.title: Speeches
references.note: University handout, no experiments: purpose as feeling, thinking or acting; state the thesis early; shorter sentences, fewer pronouns; previews and summaries; ethos, pathos and logos as teaching labels.

references.title: Oral versus Written Style
references.note: Open textbook chapter, no data: oral style uses more we, shorter thought units, repetition, contractions and familiar words; a speech is not a written text read aloud.

references.title: Ted Sorensen on Writing JFK's Speeches
references.note: A speechwriter's first-hand account in a recorded interview: years of learning the speaker's way of speaking, and a speaker who changed drafts until he was comfortable with the words. Not a technique.

references.title: The Effect of Speech Rate on Listening Comprehension of EFL Learners
references.note: Classroom experiment with 62 Iranian students of English as a foreign language, plus a literature review that reports earlier rate studies second-hand. Second-language listeners only; the captured tables are garbled, so no table figure is used.

references.authors: Philip J. Guo, Juho Kim and Rob Rubin
references.title: How Video Production Affects Student Engagement: An Empirical Study of MOOC Videos
references.note: Recorded lecture videos, not live speeches: speaking rates from 48 to 254 words per minute (mean 156, sd 31) and higher engagement with faster speakers in these courses.

references.title: Why we need to stop using that statistic about goldfish, brains and attention span
references.note: A marketing blog post that relays a BBC piece: the eight-second attention-span figure has no traceable source, and attention depends on the task. Used only to show that no hard attention limit can be quoted.

references.authors: Alex Fradera (British Psychological Society Research Digest)
references.title: Comparing Obama's and Romney's speech styles and the way their audiences react
references.note: Secondary news write-up of a study by Bull and Miskinis of 11 swing-state speeches in 2012: counts of claptraps and audience responses, correlational, and says outright that causation is untested. Figures here are the write-up's, not the paper's.

references.title: Claps and Claptrap: The Analysis of Speaker-Audience Interaction in Political Speeches
references.note: Open-access review of applause research in political speeches, mainly British and American party and campaign speeches; observational. Reports Heritage and Greatbatch's counts second-hand.

references.authors: Zhe Liu, Anbang Xu, Mengdi Zhang, Jalal Mahmud and Vibha Sinha
references.title: Fostering User Engagement: Rhetorical Devices for Applause Generation Learnt from TED Talks
references.note: arXiv preprint, abstract only: regression on transcripts of 2,135 TED talks identifies 24 rhetorical devices as triggers of applause. The devices and effect sizes were not captured.

references.authors: Aristotle, translated by W. Rhys Roberts
references.title: Rhetoric, Book I
references.note: Primary text, Book I only: three modes of persuasion and three kinds of oratory. The labels ethos, pathos and logos do not appear in this translation.

references.authors: Simone Zebregs, Bas van den Putte, Peter Neijens and Anneke de Graaf
references.title: The differential impact of statistical and narrative evidence on beliefs, attitude, and intention: a meta-analysis
references.note: Meta-analysis, mostly written health-campaign messages and no live speeches: statistical evidence stronger on beliefs and attitude, narrative stronger on intention.

references.title: How marking scripts can help you sound more natural
references.note: Radio training article on marking copy: slashes for breaths, underlines for stress, arrows for pace, phonetic spellings. Written for studio reading; nothing is measured, and its use for a hall or a prompter is an inference.

references.title: Making Events Accessible: Checklist for meetings, conferences, training, and presentations
references.note: Official checklist, qualitative: speak clearly and not too fast, pause between topics, say what is on each slide, describe visible responses, explain jargon and idioms, repeat questions. Gives no rate and no pause length.

references.title: Guidelines for Gender-Inclusive Language in English
references.note: Official guidelines for oral and written communication; gender only, and no evidence that the practices change comprehension or response.

references.title: Video Captions Benefit Everyone
references.note: Review: more than 100 studies find that captions improve comprehension of, attention to and memory for video; verbatim captions are as effective as elaborated ones.

references.title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.2.2: Captions (Prerecorded)
references.note: WCAG 2.2 Level A: captions for prerecorded audio in synchronised media, including speaker identification and meaningful sounds; synthetic speech is audio too.

references.title: Captioning Key: Presentation Rate
references.note: Caption reading-rate caps for educational media of 130, 140 and 160 words per minute by level; these bound captions, not speech.

references.title: Communication is 93% Nonverbal: An Urban Legend Proliferates
references.note: Abstract only: the 7-38-55 formula derives from two 1967 studies with serious methodological limitations and is widely misused.

references.title: The Effects of Discourse Markers on the Comprehension of Lectureships
references.note: Working paper on foreign students and university lectures; only the abstract was captured and it reports no finding, so it is not evidence that signposts help or hurt.

references.title: A test of Monroe's Motivated Sequence for its effects on ratings of message organization and attitude change
references.note: Withdrawn record, abstract only: participants read, and did not hear, a message in Monroe's order, reverse order or random order; no attitude difference. Listed so the guide can say it does not rely on it.

references.authors: Abraham Lincoln (Bliss copy, text from Wikisource)
references.title: Gettysburg Address (Bliss copy)
references.note: Primary text, 272 words: used only for short checked excerpts and a sentence-length measurement.

references.authors: A. Peter McGraw and Caleb Warren
references.title: Benign Violations: Making Immoral Behavior Funny
references.note: A theory of humour tested on small samples with moral-violation scenarios; says nothing directly about wordplay or about humour in speeches.
